newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN expected to call for extension of Haiti force.
newsitem.headline: UN expected to call for extension of Haiti force.

text.p: The United Nations was expected to call for extending the mandate of peacekeepers and international police in Haiti for another four months as Washington has recommended, diplomatic sources said on Monday.
Unknown was whether China -- which challenged the previous extension -- would agree.

A U.N report later this week was expected to call for the retention of 300 police and the 422 troops paid for by U.N. members, as requested by President Rene Preval and supported by American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson during a recent visit to the Caribbean nation.

There are some 1,300 troops and close to 300 civilian police in Haiti. More than half the troops are financed by Canada and the United States rather than by all U.N. members. It was not clear whether both countries would continue their support.
China has a history of challenging the operation because of Haiti's ties to Taiwan, which it considers a renegade province.
China's U.N. spokesman, Chen Ranfeng, told Reuters that Beijing was waiting for the report and would study it carefully.
He said China agreed to an extension of the mission last December "out of consideration of demand from the Haiti government." But it believed that extension was the final one.
"We believe the peacekeeping task has already been completed," he said.

Beijing twice threatened to veto the U.N. military component of the operation in Haiti unless its numbers were reduced, prompting Canada to rescue the mission by paying for its soldiers and then sharing the burden for its troops and those of Pakistan with the United States.

One of the operation's main tasks was to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced the previous paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide in 1991.

Aristide was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led 22,000-member multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, a number that has been steadily reduced since then.
